title: Content Moderation and Fraud Detection with ML

nodes.label: User or attacker
nodes.summary: Posts, messages, signs up or pays; attackers adapt to whatever the system keys on.

nodes.label: Product service
nodes.summary: The surface being protected (feed, messaging, checkout); calls the risk service before committing the action.

nodes.label: Risk service
nodes.summary: Synchronous scoring on the request path: under 50 ms at Facebook in 2011, under 100 ms for Stripe Radar.

nodes.label: Classifier services
nodes.summary: Models behind one interface, loaded online and never restarted (Facebook); a network-wide DNN over 1,000+ characteristics (Stripe).

nodes.label: Policy and rules engine
nodes.summary: Boolean rules over scores and features trigger responses (block, challenge, review, disable) and define holdouts; users can add allow, block, review and 3DS rules (Stripe).

nodes.label: Feature store and counters
nodes.summary: Precomputed features and velocity counters fed by feature loops that aggregate classification data and user feedback.

nodes.label: Action log stream
nodes.summary: Every action is logged; stream processors (tailers at Facebook) aggregate it into features. Our reference design uses it for asynchronous analysis.

nodes.label: Asynchronous analysis
nodes.summary: Heavier models after the fact, such as a few-shot multimodal model that takes policy text and few examples (Meta's Few-Shot Learner).

nodes.label: Human review queue
nodes.summary: Uncertain or severe cases go to reviewers; decisions and appeals become labels. Queue design is our reference design; Stripe and Facebook both route some cases to review or challenge.

nodes.label: Labels and training
nodes.summary: Reports, chargebacks, appeals and reviewer decisions; models retrain on them (Stripe found 10x more data still helped).

nodes.label: Analysts
nodes.summary: Investigate attacks, write rules and features, and ship them online without restarts.

flows.name: Scoring an action on the request path

steps.caption: A user submits a payment or a post.
The product asks the risk service before committing it.
Precomputed features and velocity counters are fetched.
Models score the action; rules turn scores into a decision.
The answer comes back within the latency budget: allow, block or challenge.
Every action and its outcome is logged.
Feature loops aggregate it, with user reports, into new features.
Heavier models review content after the fact.
Their decisions, appeals and chargebacks become labels.
Models are retrained and loaded online without restarts.
Attackers find a pattern the models miss and abuse spreads.
Analysts pick a feature expensive for the attacker to change and ship a rule online, first in shadow mode.
Once its hit rate on good users is acceptable it enforces, while new labels retrain the model.
A rule is too broad; Stripe's docs warn a bad rule can block many legitimate payments.
Block rate jumps above its baseline; the alert fires and the rule is rolled back.
Wrongly blocked cases from appeals are labelled so the next model does not learn the mistake.
